title: Use NeighborList in geometry.rdf.get_rdf
body:
I found RDFs very slow, this is because ```geometry.rdf.get_rdf``` uses ```Atoms.get_all_distances``` as a fallback (Analysis does not supply distances either).

**Unless there a reason not to that I am missing**, I have gone ahead and implemented it as the changes are not large but impactful.

That is, since we have an ```rmax``` we can use a ```NeighborList``` (where the natural cutoffs are rmax) to both speed things up and dramatically reduce memory load (see plot). I've done this in ```geometry.rdf.get_rdf```. Results are the same (tests and a quick FCC Argon test).

### Benchmark
![benchmark](/uploads/ebdc3421474c72c13de9f73378c11405/benchmark.png){width=720 height=359}

In all cases an rmax of 6 Angstroms was used.

## Reproduction

```python
from ase.geometry.rdf import get_rdf
from ase.build import bulk
from time import time
from ase.io import write

from argparse import ArgumentParser

parser = ArgumentParser()
parser.add_argument("n", type=int)
args = parser.parse_args()
atoms = bulk('Ar', 'fcc', cubic=True).repeat(args.n)
rdf, r = get_rdf(atoms, 6.0, 128)
```

```shell
for n in {4..12}
do
	res="$(/usr/bin/time -f "%e %M" python3 bench_rdf.py $n 2>&1)"
	echo $((n*n*n)) $res
done
```

comments.author: yuzie007
comments.body:
1. We should be aware of the cases that `indices` have duplicated elements due to mirror images.
To be sure that the distance matrix is consistent with `atoms.get_all_distances(mic=True)`, we need to take the image with the shortest distance.

2. Since `_` here contain the displacement vectors already, `atoms.get_distances(...)` here should be not necessary. Instead we can use e.g. `np.linalg.norm(_, axis=1)`.

I actually also think that, with `NeighborList`, we probably do not need to construct the distance matrix but rather construct the RDF from the neighbor info.

comments.author: yuzie007
comments.body:
Oh, you're right. That's my misunderstanding. The second part returns the indices for mirror images, not the distances.
So, we still need to re-compute the distances out of the `NeighborList` object.

comments.author: yuzie007
comments.body:
Thank you so much @apw951 for the MR!
The speed-up of the RDF calculation is amazing.

Actually, with `NeighborList`, we can further improve `get_rdf`.
In the present implementation (master and the present MR), only one image for each atom in the unit cell is considered.
Due to this, we need ensure that `rmax` is not too large.
On the other hand, `NeighborList` considers multiple images within the cutoff radius for each atom, and therefore we can remove the above limitation.
This allows e.g. to obtain the correct RDF from the primitive cell up to larger cutoff distance, consistently with the RDF obtained from the supercell.

From this viewpoint, I feel it is a bit detour to construct the distance matrix, which can count only one mirror image for each atom.

If you also agree, could you maybe revise the MR accordingly?
It would require a bit more changes below but makes the code much robust and flexible.

Another way to proceed the MR rather quickly may be to accept the present changes mostly as is, since the speed-up is already so fancy.
If we go this way, I would request to make an independent function for the distance-matrix construction based on `NeighborList` for better readability for future.

comments.author: apw951
comments.body:
Thanks for revieing @yuzie007, I can certainly look into doing this regarding the distance matrix, it is a detour. When I've implemented RDFs elsewhere to get around the current speed issue here, I don't bother collecting it. I just query neighbors.

Only thing is the comment above re the return value of ```nl.get_neighbors(a)```.

I will work on it.

comments.author: apw951
yuzie007
comments.body:
We can probably re-write this part using NumPy index trick as
```python
mask = atoms.numbers[j_indices] == elements[1]
j_indices = j_indices[mask]
offsets = offsets[mask]
```

comments.author: yuzie007
comments.body:
It would be better to consider mirror images for the neighbor-list-based calculations.
For this, I would suggest storing the cell shifts e.g. as
```python
j_indices, offsets = nl.get_neighbors(i)
```
where `offsets` is used below.
(Please also refer to [the usage in `emt.py`](https://gitlab.com/ase/ase/-/blob/3.26.0/ase/calculators/emt.py?ref_type=tags#L251-254).)

comments.author: yuzie007
comments.body:
`atoms.get_distances` consider only one image per atom, regardless if the neighbor list includes multiple images.

Although a bit cumbersome, we can consider the distances of multiple images with the explicit calculation e.g. as
```python
ps = atoms.positions
d = ps[j_indices] + offsets @ atoms.cell - ps[i]
distances = np.sqrt(np.add.reduce(d**2, axis=1))
# or np.linalg.norm(d, axis=1) which is a bit slower
```

(BTW I think the distance calculation functionality should rather be in the `NeighborList` class, but this should be in a separate MR.)

comments.author: yuzie007
comments.body:
We can probably write as
```python
rdf += np.bincount(indices, minlength=nbins + 1)[:nbins + 1]
```
which guarantees the RHS giving the array of the length of `nbins + 1` to be consistent with `rdf`.

comments.author: yuzie007
comments.body:
It may be safer to use `bothways=True`.
(The twice more counts are absorbed by the scaling-factor change for `norm` above.)

comments.author: yuzie007
comments.body:
Similarly to above, we may be able to write
```python
    else:
        indices = np.asarray(np.ceil(distance_matrix / dr), dtype=int)
        if elements is None:
            x = indices.ravel()
        else:
            j_indices = np.where(atoms.numbers == elements[1])[0]
            x = indices[i_indices][:, j_indices].ravel()
        rdf = np.bincount(x, minlength=nbins + 1)[:nbins + 1].astype(float)
```

comments.author: yuzie007
comments.body:
I would suggest
```python
rho = natoms / vol  # average number density
norm = 4.0 * math.pi * dr * rho * len(i_indices)
```
where the change of the scaling factor is absorbed by `bothways=True` for `NeighborList`.

comments.author: yuzie007
comments.body: Shall we test a system with two elements?

comments.author: yuzie007
comments.body:
Thank you @apw951 for the revision! Sorry for responding late.
It is nice that we can see further acceleration and memory efficiency.

I made a few additional suggestions, mostly to use NumPy array tricks.

> Handle duplicated elements due to mirror images; take the image with the shortest distance.

Regarding this, I would rather say we *should* consider real distances of mirror-image atoms, rather than mapping back to the shortest ones. As I wrote in my previous comment, this is indeed the good thing to use `NeighborList` rather than the distance matrix, where the latter can consider only the images with the shortest distance and thus required supercell construction for RDF at distant regions. On the other hand, `NeighborList` can consider this even based on the primitive cell with considering the offsets of the mirror images.
